30 March 2022 
3 
 
1. Overview 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator are respectively Profs. Marshall B. Long 
and Mitchell D. Smooke, who are both in the Department of Mechanical Engineering & Materials Science 
at Yale University.  The ISS research benefitted greatly from the work of Dr. Jesse Tinajero, who was a Yale 
postdoctoral researcher during the spaceflight operations, and Dr. Davide Giassi, who as a Yale doctoral 
student did important preparatory work.  
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including CLD Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for CLD Flame were conducted in three separate rounds of testing, where the rounds 
were respectively conducted during Increments 53-54, 55-56, and 64. The third round was limited in scope 
and was carried out with a replacement 20-slpm mass flow controller for the oxidizer coflow to make up 
for the poor coflow performance in the first two rounds. 
 
Note that there was a direct precursor to the CLD Flame investigation, namely the Structure & Liftoff In 
Combustion Experiment (SLICE), which was conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) 
during Expedition 30 in early 2012.  Prof. Long was the Principal Investigator, while Smooke, Takahashi, 
and Stocker were Co-Investigators.  For more information about SLICE, readers are encouraged to consult 
its final report.  
 
 
2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document 
(SRD) of April 2010. 
 
The proposed work will build upon our ground-based microgravity studies in which advanced 
adaptive (parallel) computational algorithms and multidimensional imaging techniques were 
performed to characterize buoyant and nonbuoyant diffusion flames.  The computational work 
has facilitated the development of detailed soot models while the experimental work performed 
has built expertise in bringing two-dimensional, laboratory-quality diagnostics to a microgravity 
environment.  The experimental results of our previous microgravity combustion studies have 
provided the most rigorous testing of our combustion models to date.  Experiments were 
performed on the KC-135 of a nitrogen-diluted methane coflow laminar diffusion flame to 
measure flame chemiluminescence, temperature, major species, and soot distributions.  The 
results compared well with computations in the moderately dilute cases, but discrepancies were 
revealed in the case of the more dilute flames, particularly with the observed lift-off heights and

extinction limits.  Additionally, the weak flames and the sooting flames were observed to be 
sensitive to the presence of g-jitter, making clear analysis difficult.  It is at these extremes of the 
fuel dilution spectrum that the most interesting effects can be observed.  Further, by extending 
the studies over a broad range of conditions, discrepancies between measurement and 
computation have been discovered that previous laboratory studies of this flame failed to reveal. 
 
We propose to concentrate this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution 
spectrum – namely dilute flames near extinction and highly-sooting pure-fuel flames.  Previous 
work has shown that both weak flames and highly sooting flames require long periods of “clean” 
microgravity to reach a steady state.  The conditions aboard the International Space Station (ISS) 
will be ideal in this regard.  The intended flight experiments will provide insights into flame 
stability, extinction, and soot processes that are unavailable in ground-based microgravity 
facilities. 
 
Our project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot 
submodels that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high 
soot loading levels.  The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be 
important for achieving both goals.  Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene 
diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions.  For the more dilute flames, measurements 
will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height 
and flame shape as extinction limits are approached.  The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-
rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to 
determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions.  Flame temperatures in nonsooting 
regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry.  Based on observations, modifications 
can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results.  If the 
overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the 
computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that 
cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment. 
 
B. Rationale for Microgravity 
This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.6) of the experiment’s SRD 
from April 2010.  References are not included in this document but can be found in the SRD. 
 
The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical 
kinetics in diffusion flames is central to nearly all aspects of combustion research: in the modeling 
of turbulent reacting flows, in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative 
transfer take place, and in the prediction of pollutant formation.  In addition, an understanding of 
those factors that affect flame extinction is critical in the suppression of fires, in improving engine 
efficiency, and in reducing emissions.  While normal gravity combustion studies can provide 
important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces can often 
complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results.  For example, 
most practical combustors are turbulent, and consequently momentum-dominated, while most 
laboratory-scale research burners have significant buoyancy contributions.  Therefore, studies of 
microgravity flames are of direct relevance to research in turbulent combustion since buoyancy 
effects are eliminated.  In addition to being inherently simpler, nonbuoyant flames have the 
advantage that hot gases are not accelerated by gravitational forces, which results in longer 
residence times and larger length scales.  These longer residence times have been shown to result

ACME/CLD Flame Final Report (2022) 
 
30 March 2022 
5 
 
in higher soot loading in microgravity flames compared to their normal gravity counterparts.  The 
larger spatial scales allow improved experimental resolution, which in turn gives a clearer, more 
spatially distinct view of the progress from soot inception and growth to eventual burnout.  Thus, 
microgravity data on sooting flames will provide a wide range of well-resolved conditions that will 
be critical for the development of submodels for soot formation that are capable of predicting 
both high and low soot loading levels. 
 
As we have seen from our previous microgravity work (see Fig. 2), very weak flames can be 
stabilized in a microgravity that extinguish under normal gravity conditions.  These flames are free 
of buoyant coupling of the flowfield or buoyancy-induced asymmetries, which can complicate 
comparisons between models and experiments under normal gravity conditions.  For these 
flames, small changes in the chemical kinetics were seen to have a significant effect on the 
agreement between measured and computed flame structure and lift-off height.  Once again, the 
microgravity environment allows us to investigate a wider range of flow and dilution conditions 
than would be accessible in a normal gravity environment; these data will be invaluable for our 
overall goal of developing improved kinetic mechanisms applicable to a wide range of combustion 
conditions. 
 
Section 1 discusses our previous experimental work in microgravity, which was carried out aboard 
the KC-135. The KC-135 was chosen over other ground-based microgravity facilities (such as a 
drop towers) due to the relatively long periods of microgravity available, which allowed adequate 
time for flame stabilization and integration of weak signals necessary for good signal/noise. 
However, the work also showed that both very dilute flames near extinction and sooty flames are 
sensitive to the g-jitter aboard the KC-135. 
 
Highly dilute fuel mixtures, which can only be stabilized under microgravity conditions, cannot be 
lit until microgravity conditions are reached. After ignition is established, the ignition source must 
be removed, and the flame allowed to stabilize.  Further, data acquisition of flame 
chemiluminescence requires total integration times of ~10 seconds to obtain sufficient 
signal/noise for good results when a tomographic inversion is used to reconstruct a two-
dimensional cross section.  Because flame luminosity is integrated along a line-of-sight, a low 
numerical aperture must be used, which results in a small optical throughput.  The combination 
of the time requirements for flame ignition, stabilization, and signal integration makes this 
experiment a poor candidate for drop tower facilities.  The most dilute of these mixtures 
previously studied exhibited unstable behavior aboard the KC-135 similar to that observed for 
sooting flames, with the lift-off height changing by several mm over the course of a parabola.   The 
longer periods of comparatively jitter-free μg available on the ISS will be critical for quantitative 
characterization of these weak flames.  A better understanding of the limits of extinction in these 
relatively cool flames will be important for improving kinetics mechanisms and understanding 
pathways to extinction.  Additionally, longer uninterrupted periods of microgravity will provide 
the opportunity to study a wider range of flow conditions without having to reset the 
experimental apparatus. 
 
For sooting flames, a number of experiments have shown that the overall flame structure is 
markedly different in space than in the shorter-duration periods of microgravity available in 
ground-based facilities [9].  Candle flames that were sooty in normal gravity, during aircraft 
testing, and in the high-quality microgravity of drop facilities, were observed to be blue in testing

on orbit in the Space Shuttle and Mir space station [36, 37].  If the experimental results obtained 
are to be used to validate the soot models, the long-term, low-jitter environment of space will be 
required. 
 
C. Science Objectives 
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.3) of the 
experiment’s SRD from April 2010. 
 
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational 
models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: 
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off 
heights, temperatures and extinction limits. 
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas 
temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, 
and soot volume fractions. 
A more complete listing of the specific flame conditions that we will investigate is given in Sections 
2.4 and 3.3. 
 
D. Science Success Criteria 
This text is from the CLD Flame portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME Integrated 
Science Requirements Document (ISRD, ACME-SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is revision B of 
the version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR). 
 
Success of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame experiment will be judged on meeting the stated 
experimental objectives by acquiring results that lead to the stated data end products.  Three 
different levels of success – minimum, high, and complete success – are defined. An additional 
level of success is defined as satisfying our overall project goals, which is not required for complete 
experimental success. 
 
6.1.1. Minimum Success 
Minimum success is defined to mean acquisition of sufficient scientific data from the 
experiment to perform a direct comparison with the numerical computations and publish 
at least one journal article.  This minimal level of success may be achieved by obtaining 
basic information about the flame characteristics from the color images or UV images, 
possibly for a subset of the flame conditions outlined above.  Meaningful subsets of the 
data might include data from a single fuel (methane or ethylene, but not both) or from 
either weak or sooting flames, but not both.  Data would remain valuable for comparisons 
with computational models, albeit not as complete as would be desirable.  For example, 
minimum success might come from obtaining data as follows: 
1. Color images of nonsooting flames only (SDEP A1). 
2. UV images of OH* luminosity from nonsooting flames (towards SDEP A2). 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science data end 
products including the following: 
- 
Observation of lift-off heights as a function of dilution level (SDEP A4). 
- 
Observation of extinction limits as a function of dilution level (SDEP A6).

6.1.2. High Success 
High success is defined  to mean acquisition of sufficient scientific data from the 
experiment to perform a direct comparison with the numerical computations and publish 
several journal articles.  In addition to the information obtained for a minimum level of 
success, a high level of success may be achieved by obtaining more detailed information 
about the flame characteristics from UV images for species concentrations and from soot 
diagnostics for soot volume fraction (for example): 
1. 2D images of soot laser extinction and associated reference images 
2. 2D images of multi-color soot luminosity (from pyrometry data). 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science 
data end products including the following: 
- 
2D images of soot volume fraction (SDEP B11). 
- 
2D images of soot temperatures (SDEP B9). 
6.1.3.  Complete Success 
Complete success is defined to mean acquisition of all data related to the experimental 
objectives.  In addition to the information obtained for a high level of success, a complete 
level of success may be achieved by obtaining complete information about the flame 
characteristics using the available diagnostic techniques, including full information on 
temperatures, extinction and sooting tendencies across the full range of flow conditions: 
1. Multi-color images of TFP data, including reference images. 
2. Images of soot extinction representing the peak soot volume fraction, including 
reference images. 
3. Soot luminosity images representing the peak soot temperature, including 
reference images. 
This would provide data that would allow us to determine several of our science data end 
products including the following: 
- 
Radial temperature profiles from TFP (SDEP A7 and B8). 
- 
Combined temperature fields from soot pyrometry and TFP (SDEP A7 and B8 with 
B9). 
- 
Peak soot volume fraction as a function of fuel dilution over the full range of flow 
velocities (SDEP B12). 
- 
Peak temperature as a function of fuel dilution over the full range of flow 
velocities (SDEP A8 and B10). 
 
 
3. Hardware Overview 
A. General Description 
This section is copied from section 2.A of the April 2021 version of ‘ACME Engineering 
Implementation’ which should be consulted for additional details.  References to other sections 
within the boxed text of this section refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document.

This section provides a general description a general description of the ACME engineering from 
the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014. 
 
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the 
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017.  As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards.   Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description.  As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.  Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS. 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1

and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.  
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests.  The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.  Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.  However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the 
exception of the latter’s first day testing.  The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip.  
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.  The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines.  The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy.  The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames, 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments.  Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases.  CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME

will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent.  Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit.  Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 
maximum of 5 slpm.  ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control.  
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit.  All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.  Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.  However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror).  Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development.  The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.  Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images.  The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.  Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.  The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24].  Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM).  A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission.  However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space.  The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center.  Its 
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.   
 
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second.  The clear “filter” is 
of fused silica.  Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added 
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the 
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature 
determination.  Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high

definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions.   
For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).   
 
Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.   
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band.  This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps).  Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF.  Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers.  The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.  During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF.  An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. 
 
In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but 
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements.  For an 
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers:   
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry 
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750.  
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S-type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. 
 
Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total 
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array.  
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest 
downstream position.  Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and 
subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and at least the initial testing for the Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). 
 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction.  This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the 
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at 
opposite windows.  The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps.  Thus far, the primary 
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for 
determination of the droplet burning rate. 
 
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much, 
but not all, of ACME’s operations.  In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used 
without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera

B. Hardware Shortcomings 
The primary hardware challenge for CLD Flame was the unsatisfactory performance of the Mass 
Flow Controllers (MFCs).  In particular, the MFC initially used for the oxidizer coflow behaved as if 
it momentary stuck in a few places, where the flow rate wouldn’t linearly ramp with time when 
commanded.  It tended to stick in some places and then abruptly overshoot where that was 
sometimes seen to extinguish the flame.   This prevented determination of extinction limits and 
led to the decision to prepare and launch a replacement MFC and add a short third round of CLD 
Flame testing.  The replacement was installed on 3 Feb. 2021 (21034).  The replacement’s control 
of the flow rate was much better as was verified during MFC testing on the subsequent day.  
However, it must be recognized that the majority of the investigation’s tests were carried out with 
the ill-behaving oxidizer MFC. 
 
Besides the issue with the oxidizer MFC, the fuel and especially nitrogen flows were sometimes 
found to oscillate.  Adjustments were subsequently made to (1) the cracking settings that control 
when the MFC valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) settings.  While the 
MFC tuning has been beneficial in some cases, it has not eliminated all gas flow problems.  It was 
seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was implemented 
so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame measurements.  That approach was 
partially successful and was introduced between CLD Flame’s first and second rounds.  Later, a 
procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to each test was also implemented between CLD Flame’s 
second and third rounds. 
 
Successful ignition was sometime an issue, especially early in the CLD Flame testing, where it was 
the first ACME experiment for which tests were conducted.  As a result, CLD Flame encountered

4. Preliminary Results  
A. Changed Test Plans 
The most significant change in CLD Flame plans resulted from the poor performance of the Mass 
Flow Controller (MFC) used for the oxidizer coflow.  Its inability to provide a smooth ramped 
increase to the flow rate, and thus coflow velocity, prevented determination of extinction limits 
for a range of flame conditions.  As a temporary way to partially mitigate the science loss, tests 
were sometimes conducted where the coflow velocity was reduced rather than increased.  But 
given the science loss, the decision was made to prepare and launch a replacement MFC.  Those 
tests were ultimately conducted in early 2021, whereas the earlier tests were carried out in late 
2017 and 2018. 
 
Unwanted oscillations in the fuel and nitrogen flow were sometimes encountered and those led 
to operational changes which were partially successful.  The nitrogen oscillations were often 
observed to damp with time and the software script controlling the CLD Flame tests was modified 
between the first and second round of testing to accommodate a pre-flow of nitrogen with the 
goal of allowing any oscillations to diminish prior to the ignition of the flame.  Furthermore, a 
practice of re-zeroing the MFCs shortly before the start of each test was adopted.  Besides these 
measures, on-orbit adjustments were made to the MFCs’ cracking and Proportional-Integral-
Derivative (PID) settings. 
 
The use of long exposure times for the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) was adopted because of 
the dim nature of the microgravity flames.  The planned use of the blue green BG7 Schott glass 
filter with the DataCam for pyrometry was largely abandoned because the combination of the 
filter thickness and the added antireflective (AR) coating caused to great a reduction in the red 
color plane.  As a result of wear and breakage, different arrays of ceramic fibers for Thin Filament 
Pyrometry (TFP) were used during the three rounds of testing.   In the first round, the fifth fiber 
position (farthest downstream) had a platinum wire instead of a 14-micron Silicon Carbide (SiC) 
ceramic fiber like those in the four other positions.  In the second round, an array with five SiC 
fibers was used, while in the third round the array had only three fibers because two had broken. 
 
Testing began with the red filter removed from the High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera 
so that it could be used to image the flame rather than light extinction, e.g., for soot visualization 
and potential measurement, using the CIR illumination package.  However, it was discovered that 
the HiBMs camera was insensitive to blue light, where that’s the natural color of the hydrocarbon 
flames tested (neglecting any soot).  Therefore, after the first of CLD Flame testing, the red filter 
corresponding to the illumination package was installed to enable imaging with light extinction.  
However, CLD Flame employed a method featuring absolute light calibration to determine the 
soot volume fraction from the DataCam imaging.  As a result, HiBMs images were of limited value 
and were only sometimes saved or even recorded.  The camera wasn’t used at all during the third 
round of testing.

was in use on 22 Dec. 2017 (17356) which added parameters for specifying the gain for each of

D. Surprises and New Discoveries  
There are many aspects to diffusion flame combustion that are still not well understood at a 
fundamental level, and microgravity combustion has proven to be an effective environment from 
which to gain a deeper understanding.  The CLD Flame research has shown that microgravity 
flames can be 4-8 times sootier than their normal gravity counterparts and that the distribution 
of peak soot shifts from the centerline of the flame at normal gravity to the wings in microgravity.  
Such changes in the soot field are consistent with results from a variety of experiments on coflow 
flames in both ground- and space-based venues as well as different mass flow rates, burner 
diameters and fuels.  The increased soot loading and flame residence times lead to lower flame 
temperature in microgravity due to increased radiative losses.  
One of the project goals of CLD Flame was obtain quantitative measurements of sooting coflow 
diffusion flames in both normal and microgravity conditions on a burner with well characterized 
boundary conditions, and to use those measurements to improve computational models.  
Previous work had shown that existing computational models were unable to predict accurately 
the behavior of these systems.  With the new data provided, efforts are underway to generate 
new simulations matching the ACME test conditions under 1 g and 0 g conditions.  
A key element in the CLD Flame dataset is the availability of carefully measured boundary 
conditions, which are critical for comparison with computational models.  These were measured 
on both the ground-based copy as well as the flight copy of the coflow burners.  Figure 15 shows 
an example of one such velocity profile measured under cold-flow conditions at 0.5 mm above 
the fuel tube.  This was used as an input boundary condition for calculations of pure ethylene 
flames on 1 g and 0 g, and comparisons were made to the experimental data.

E. Accomplishment of Approved Objectives 
CLD Flame had two main objectives as follows: 
 
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames methane and ethylene, as a function 
of velocity and fuel dilution. 
 
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of methane and ethylene diffusion flames with long 
residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution. 
 
Through the three rounds of testing of CLD Flame, both objectives were achieved, as seen in the 
examples above.  The first round of testing effectively began in January 2018 and concentrated 
on measurements in dilute methane flames, as well as characterization and calibration of the 
imaging systems.  The second round of experiments began in May 2018, and provided results on 
sooting methane and ethylene flames, as well as some data on weak, lifted ethylene flames.  
Because of issues related to the stability of the mass flow controllers, the quality of data on the 
extinction limits of the dilute methane and ethylene flames was not optimal.  Therefore, a third

F. Additional Objectives Achieved 
Computational and Experimental Study of the Effects of Pressure and Fuel Dilution 
Since the CLD Flame experiments were carried out in an enclosed pressure vessel, there was an 
increase in pressure during each test due to the addition of fresh gas into the chamber (primarily 
from the coflow).  To understand better the effects of this increasing pressure, a combined 
computational and experimental investigation was conducted to characterize the influences of 
pressure, as well as fuel stream dilution on the structure, shape, and sooting behavior of coflow 
methane–air laminar diffusion flames under normal gravity conditions.  A series of 72 methane–
air coflow laminar diffusion flames with four levels of nitrogen dilution in the fuel stream (50, 55, 
60, and 65% methane) and 18 levels of pressure (1.0 to 2.7 atm in 0.1 atm increments) were 
assessed.  In general, very good agreement between the computations and the experiments was 
achieved for the temperature, the flame shape, and the soot volume fraction, and the numerical 
model successfully captured the effects of varying pressure and fuel stream dilution. The major 
conclusions of this research were as follows:  
 
• The maximum temperature increases with increasing methane concentration or 
pressure.   
• The lift-off height decreases significantly with increasing pressure, the modified flame 
length is roughly independent of pressure, and the flame radius decreases with pressure 
approximately as P−1/2.   
• The pressure and fuel stream dilution significantly affect the spatial distribution and the 
peak value of the soot volume fraction.  
 
Results of this study were published in Combustion Theory and Modelling. 
 
Software Development and Documentation 
As part of our NASA diagnostics development work, techniques were implemented for 
quantitative measurements of soot temperature, soot volume fraction, thin-filament fiber 
temperature, and concentration of CH* in axisymmetric flames.  These techniques require 
software for image acquisition and processing as well as careful characterization of the detection 
systems used.  The bulk of this is done using image processing software developed in our labs over 
a period of more than thirty years.  The “OMA” software has undergone continuous revision and 
extension and a version of the software for the Mac operating system has been available as open 
source since 2005 (http://oma-x.org).  All the ACME experiments used the same detectors, and 
many can use the same processing methods that we have developed to handle the raw data.  The

G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
The main product from CLD Flame is a comprehensive dataset of microgravity and normal gravity 
coflow methane and ethylene diffusion flames.  These include weak, lifted flames near extinction, 
under a variety of fuel dilution levels and flow conditions.  The highly diluted, lifted flames tend 
to be non-sooting and differences in liftoff height and flame stability between 1 g and 0 g are 
significant (e.g., see Fig. 10 above).  This data will provide a stringent test for computational 
models seeking to predict flame extinction.  At the other end of the fuel dilution spectrum, the 
dataset includes robust, sooting flames, with different flow conditions and dilution levels, which 
provide different flame heights and levels of soot loading.  Once again, the contrast between 1 g 
and 0 g flames is remarkable and the lack of agreement between experimental and computational 
results points to deficiencies in current models of soot formation. 
 
The raw image data from CLD Flame has been processed to provide quantitative data on 
temperature in both the non-sooting and sooting flames using thin-filament and soot pyrometry, 
respectively.  An absolute light calibration of the camera and optical train allows further 
quantification of CH chemiluminescence in weak flames, as well as soot volume fraction in the 
case of sooting flames.  The flow conditions are matched in the 1 g and 0 g datasets, and in both 
cases, detailed near-field velocity measurements have been made.  These boundary conditions 
are critical as input to computational models wishing to compare experimental and predicted 
results. 
 
In addition to the raw data from 1 g and 0 g flames, processed data in the form of computer-
readable data files as well as final figures have been uploaded to the NASA website.  Examples of

I.  Introduction 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is conducted in the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via 
Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, the flame - burning a gaseous fuel 
- is surrounded by air flowing in the same direction as the fuel.  More specifically, the gaseous 
fuel flows from an inner tube which is centered within a much larger outer tube, where a 21/79 
mixture of oxygen and nitrogen (on a volume basis) flows from the annulus.  The testing is 
generally conducted where the fuel and velocities are matched.  Measurements are made of 
flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability.  Conducting the 
tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis, enabling new understanding

and the development of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on 
Earth. 
 
The overall goal is to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes 
controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., 
stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal 
radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.  Such understanding allows for detailed 
computational predictions, e.g., of pollutant formation, and enables the improvement of 
combustion efficiency and reduction of pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. 
 
Research conducted in microgravity has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly 
lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute 
flames that are near extinction. The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the 
range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally 
verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.  The dependence of normal coflow 
flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution is carefully examined for flames at both very dilute 
and highly sooting conditions.  Measurements are made of the structure of methane and 
ethylene flames in an air coflow, where the fuels are often diluted with nitrogen. Lifted flames 
are used as the basis for the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner. The 
results of this experiment are directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent 
combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational 
models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, CLD Flame has the following objectives: 
A. Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as 
a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off 
heights, temperatures and extinction limits. 
B. Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas 
temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, 
and soot volume fractions. 
 
The experiment characterizes the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing 
region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel (including nitrogen 
dilution) and flow conditions. The velocity limits where the flame detaches from the burner and 
later extinguishes are similarly identified as a function of the fuel.  An understanding of lifting 
and lifted behavior is valuable, because of the importance of flame stability to the safe operation 
of practical combustion systems. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be

studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and

gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
A precursor to the CLD Flame experiment was carried out during Expedition 30 in early 2012, 
namely the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE).  The SLICE tests were conducted 
in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the hardware from the Smoke Point In Coflow 
Experiment (SPICE).  The SPICE hardware was based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) 
investigation which was conducted in the Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) on STS-87 in 1997.  The ELF, 
SPICE, and SLICE investigated coflow flames by placement of a gas-jet burner within a small fan-
driven flow duct open to the glovebox facility.  Meanwhile, the CLD Flame experiment is carried 
out with a coflow burner within a sealed 100-liter chamber, with a coflow of compressed gas. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
CLD Flame and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS 
crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The 
most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) 
and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 53-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed (in the analog 
ops video) that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
A total of 292 flames were ignited in two rounds of on-orbit testing, with 130 and 162 
respectively in the first and second rounds of the CLD Flame experiment.  Neglecting 
hardware set-up and engineering preparation, the first round took place from Nov. 2017 
to Feb. 2018, i.e., in Increments 53 and 54.  ACME testing subsequently shifted to the 
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment, and 
afterward returned for a  second round of CLD Flame tests, which took place from May to 
September 2018, i.e., during Increments 55 and 56.  The ‘interruption’ in the CLD Flame 
testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the 
initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize 
its scientific outcome. 
 
CLD Flame does not have subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because 
of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel 
mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and 
nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with 
methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a 
volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for CLD Flame, where all of the ISS results 
are electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
CLD Flame tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software 
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a 
result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   The aborts 
normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These are infrequent, 
but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter

energized while remaining within the flame.  The script running the tests is normally

discussed).   Furthermore, the igniter tip is proactively replaced on a periodic basis, 
when the crew are making other changes on the ACME chamber insert.  As a result, 
no additional ACME igniter tips have failed thus far.

C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited far exceeds the originally planned tests that were specified 
as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD).  In contrast, 
to the 82 CLD Flame tests identified as required in the ISRD, 292 flames were ignited in 
Increments 53-56 for the CLD Flame experiment.  In other words, 250% more flames were 
ignited than had been planned. 
 
The breadth of fuel concentrations tests was also much greater than those originally 
planned, i.e., were required in the ACME ISRD.  The required methane tests were limited 
to low fuel concentrations (on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of 15%, 20%, 
and 30% and high concentrations of 80%, 90%, and 100%.  Methane concentrations 
between 30% and 80% were specified as desired or highly desired.  While tests were 
conducted at required concentrations, they were also conducted at intermediate 
concentrations, e.g., 40% and 50% methane.  Meanwhile, the required ethylene tests 
were at concentrations (again on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of only 10%, 
15%, 20%, and 50%.  Tests were conducted at those four concentrations, at intermediate 
concentrations between 20% and 50% (e.g., 30% and 40%), and at higher concentrations,

Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is

some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Preliminary tests with flames are sometimes conducted on days during testing and tuning 
(i.e., adjustment) of mass flow controllers, where the recorded image data is typically 
limited to just the analog operations (ops) camera, i.e., which is downlinked in near real 
time.  The six flames ignited on Aug. 29, 2018 (18241) are an example of such testing.  
These tests are conducted to check flow performance, verify ignition parameters, etc.   In 
other words, they are conducted to gain basic information to prepare for subsequent 
tests. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  In this regard, 
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).  
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and CLD Flame is considered to be highly successful with the exception of

Due to the importance of fiber measurements for analyzing the ACME data camera’s

initial focus has been on fiber test points. For some of our weak flames with low overall

I.  Introduction 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is conducted in the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via 
Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, the flame - burning a gaseous fuel 
- is surrounded by air flowing in the same direction as the fuel.  More specifically, the gaseous 
fuel flows from an inner tube which is centered within a much larger outer tube, where a 21/79 
mixture of oxygen and nitrogen (on a volume basis) flows from the annulus.  The testing is

generally conducted where the fuel and velocities are matched.  Measurements are made of 
flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability.  Conducting the 
tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis, enabling new understanding 
and the development of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for use on 
Earth. 
 
The overall goal is to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes 
controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., 
stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal 
radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.  Such understanding allows for detailed 
computational predictions, e.g., of pollutant formation, and enables the improvement of 
combustion efficiency and reduction of pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. 
 
Research conducted in microgravity has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly 
lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute 
flames that are near extinction. The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the 
range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally 
verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.  The dependence of normal coflow 
flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution is carefully examined for flames at both very dilute 
and highly sooting conditions.  Measurements are made of the structure of methane and 
ethylene flames in an air coflow, where the fuels are often diluted with nitrogen. Lifted flames 
are used as the basis for the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner. The 
results of this experiment are directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent 
combustion, ignition, flame stability, and more. 
 
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational 
models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, CLD Flame has the following objectives: 
A. Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as 
a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off 
heights, temperatures and extinction limits. 
B. Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a 
function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas 
temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, 
and soot volume fractions. 
 
The experiment characterizes the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing 
region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel (including nitrogen 
dilution) and flow conditions. The velocity limits where the flame detaches from the burner and 
later extinguishes are similarly identified as a function of the fuel.  An understanding of lifting 
and lifted behavior is valuable, because of the importance of flame stability to the safe operation 
of practical combustion systems. 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,

gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity 
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
A precursor to the CLD Flame experiment was carried out during Expedition 30 in early 2012, 
namely the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE).  The SLICE tests were conducted 
in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the hardware from the Smoke Point In Coflow 
Experiment (SPICE).  The SPICE hardware was based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) 
investigation which was conducted in the Middeck Glovebox (MGBX) on STS-87 in 1997.  The ELF, 
SPICE, and SLICE experiments investigated coflow flames by placement of a gas-jet burner within 
a small fan-driven flow duct open to the glovebox facility.  Meanwhile, the CLD Flame experiment 
is carried out with a coflow burner within a sealed 100-liter chamber, with a coflow of 
compressed gas. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
CLD Flame and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS 
crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The 
most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) 
and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or 
soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 53-56, where the console commanding 
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed (in the analog 
ops video) that the flame had extinguished. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.

A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
Neglecting hardware set-up and engineering preparation, the first round took place from 
Nov. 2017 to Feb. 2018, during Increments 53-54, when 130 methane flames were 
ignited.  ACME testing subsequently shifted to the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar 
Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment, and afterward returned for a  second 
round of CLD Flame tests, which took place from May to September 2018, during 
Increments 55-56, when 162 ethylene flames were ignited.  The ‘interruption’ in the CLD 
Flame testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review 
the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to 
maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
Poor performance in ramping the oxidizer coflow during early testing inhibited 
determination of extinction limits.  The decision was made to launch a replacement Mass 
Flow Controller (MFC) and conduct a limited third round of tests to address that 
shortcoming.  The third round with the replacement MFC was conducted in Feb.-March 
2021, during Increment 64, when 52 ethylene and methane flames were ignited.  As a 
result, a total of 344 flames were ignited during the three rounds and five increments. 
 
CLD Flame does not have subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because 
of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel 
mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and 
nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with 
methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a 
volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME 
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing 
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.  In all cases, 
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for CLD Flame, where all of the ISS results 
are electronically transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently 
planned ACME experiments.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
CLD Flame tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software 
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a 
result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.   The aborts 
normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1.  These are 
infrequent, but there are some days when tests have aborted repeatedly.  
 
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of 
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been 
sufficiently primed.  Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the 
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of 
the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter 
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.  
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* 
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* 
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited 
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible 
spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to 
false ignition detection. 
 
Ignition failure repeatedly occurred in early testing, where it was determined in 
December 2017 that the igniter arm was not properly aligned with the burner.  This 
was corrected by astronaut Joe Acaba with the help of Mark Vande Hei on 5 Jan. 2018 
(18005).  The alignment helped enable the ignition of 57 flames that month in contrast 
to the 15 and 11 flames ignited in November and December 2017, respectively.

MFC valves open and (2) their Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) settings.  This

oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was implemented so that 
the oscillations would typically end before the flame measurements.  That approach

C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited far exceeds the originally planned tests that were specified 
as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD).  In contrast, 
to the 82 CLD Flame tests identified as required in the ISRD, 344 flames were ignited for 
the CLD Flame experiment.  While not all of them provided useful data, 320% more flames 
were ignited than had been planned. 
 
The breadth of fuel concentrations tests was also much greater than those originally 
planned, i.e., were required in the ACME ISRD.  The required methane tests were limited 
to low fuel concentrations (on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of 15%, 20%, 
and 30% and high concentrations of 80%, 90%, and 100%.  Methane concentrations 
between 30% and 80% were specified as desired or highly desired.  While tests were 
conducted at required concentrations, they were also conducted at intermediate 
concentrations, e.g., 40% and 50% methane.  Meanwhile, the required ethylene tests 
were at concentrations (again on a volume basis, with a balance of nitrogen) of only 10%, 
15%, 20%, and 50% and during dynamic dilution toward even lower concentrations.  Tests 
were conducted at those four concentrations, at intermediate concentrations between 
20% and 50% (e.g., 30% and 40%), and at higher concentrations, e.g., 60%, 80%, and 
100%.  While tests with 20% and 30% ethylene were specified as desired, there were

discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 ceased to work during the second round of testing, 
preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination package.  
Those are not critical for CLD Flame, so tests continued without their use.  Similarly, the 
HiBMs camera and illumination package were not used during the round 3 testing.  
 
Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is 
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be 
managed per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice 
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing 
within the project constraints. 
 
Preliminary tests with flames are sometimes conducted on days during testing and tuning 
(i.e., adjustment) of mass flow controllers, where the recorded image data is typically 
limited to just the analog operations (ops) camera, i.e., which is downlinked in near real 
time.  The six flames ignited on 29 Aug. 2018 (18241) are an example of such testing.  
These tests are conducted to check flow performance, verify ignition parameters, etc.   In 
other words, they are conducted to gain basic information to prepare for subsequent 
tests. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality. 
 
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there 
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available 
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).  Note that 
although the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is 
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) it was not utilized for CLD Flame 
(or any ACME) testing because of the crew time needed to enable and disable the 
isolation before and after testing. 
 
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has 
been secured and CLD Flame, as a whole, is considered to be highly successful.

The CLD Flame experiment produced a comprehensive data set of microgravity methane 
and ethylene flames over three rounds of testing.  Round one focused on methane flames 
while looking at the full range of dilution from pure fuel to near the dilution extinction

A substantial amount of effort has been made to evaluate the absolute light calibration 
method which is needed to perform quantitative flame measurements.  Because the light 
calibration was performed through thin filament pyrometry (TFP), improvements were

Quantitative measurements have been made on tests from all three rounds.  Light

Measurements of flame characteristics, such as flame heights, flame structures and lift-

In parallel with the microgravity data, substantial efforts have been made on the normal 
gravity experimentation front, where many of the flame conditions were recreated on 
earth to determine the effects of gravity.  The measurements performed include flame

ethylene flames, and flame images to analyze flame characteristics.

Microgravity flames were observed to grow taller as a function of fuel concentration 
compared to normal gravity flames.  The pure fuel condition in Fig. 7(d) and 8(d) showed 
a height difference of nearly 1 cm.  Classic flame models, such as the Burke and Schumann 
flame model, have predicted that flame heights should be unaffected by gravity, however, 
these models have not carefully accounted for temperature dependent transport 
properties.  
 
Because the lack of buoyancy increases residence times, the soot loads in microgravity 
are higher, and thus, thermal radiative energy losses are higher in microgravity. The 
flames in microgravity are measured to have soot loads a factor of five to eight times 
higher in microgravity than in normal gravity. This results in the microgravity flames 
decreasing in temperature more rapidly as the flames grow in volume and as soot loads 
increase.  
 
The measured soot temperatures were used to estimate transport properties, which were 
then applied to a nondimensional analysis of flame heights proposed by Lin and Faeth 
(AIAA J. 37, 759–765, 1999).  The results are shown in Fig. 9.  An empirical constant, Cf, is 
determined through a linear-least-squares fit with the experimental data, where a value 
of Cf equal to unity represents a perfect fit to the theoretical flame model.  This figure 
demonstrates that when accounting for temperature dependent transport properties, 
the flame heights of microgravity and normal gravity flames can be effectively described 
by this simple flame model, since Cf is nearly unity in both cases.

were asymmetric. Finally, when the electric field is deactivated, the soot streams from the top of

to control soot production in flames. Results could ultimately lead to more efficient and less 
polluting combustion technology for use on Earth.

focused on acquiring benchmark flame data on the two extremes of high dilution and heavy soot 
production and using that information to improve computational models. The modeling could enable 
improved design tools for practical terrestrial combustion leading to improved efficiency and reduced 
pollutant emission.   
 
The coflow burner used for this experiment can simultaneously flow air and a gaseous fuel mixture. In 
some tests, the flame detaches and lifts away from the burner because the flow velocities are too high to 
sustain combustion. The flames on the space shuttle’s main engines are an example of this phenomenon. 
When the flame is attached to the burner, the fuel and oxygen are separated by the flame sheet. But as 
the flame lifts, the two reactants can increasingly mix, which changes the nature of the flame.

of the flame temperature. Other tests were focused on optical measurement of the excited molecule CH*, 
which emits a blue photon as it drops in energy. It naturally occurs in hydrocarbon flames and is the 
primary cause of their blue color. On GMT 048, Victor Glover replaced the gas bottles at CIR Manifold #2 
and CIR Manifold #4 to support continuation of CLD Flame test points.

microgravity, 16 flames of 40% methane were ignited. In some tests, the flow rates of the fuel and 
simultaneous flow of air were kept steady. In other tests, the air velocity was increased during the test or 
the fuel was diluted while holding the velocities steady.

On GMT 062, the final test points were performed for ACME CLD Flame (Coflow Laminar Diffusion). The 
Principal Investigator, Marshall Long from Yale University, considers the experiment to have been very 
successful. On this day, 11 flames were ignited, which contributed to the over 300 that were ignited for

normal gravity. Steady microgravity flames are also more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the 
lack of buoyancy. We have gathered a superior set of experimental data to be used for improving our 
ability to computationally model highly diluted flames. This capability could be implemented in design 
tools resulting in more efficient and less polluting combustion here on Earth.

Appendix M. Summary of the ISS data collection 
The CLD Flame data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the 
other ACME experiments.  To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were 
subsequently transported to the ground.  
 
The CLD Flame image data includes images from the following cameras: 
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but 
those settings were consistent within each individual test) 
2. CFI intensified camera, typically used with a CH* filter (and likely always for CLD Flame) 
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the 
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off 
 
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and 
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format.  In contrast, the analog video was 
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. 
 
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software 
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). 
 
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through 
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).
